lesson.title: The Personal 'a'
lesson.subtitle: Placing 'a' before specific human direct objects: veo a María, conozco a tu hermano, invito a mi amigo

hook.title: Respecting People in Grammar
hook.content: Think of the personal 'a' as a grammatical bow of respect Whenever a verb's direct action lands on a specific human being (ver 'to see', conocer 'to know', invitar 'to invite', visitar 'to visit', ayudar 'to help'), place **a** before the person! And remember: if the person is masculine singular with el (el profesor, el señor), **a + el** still contracts to **al**: Veo al señor ('I see the gentleman')!

pattern.title: Thing vs Person Side by Side
pattern.content:
• Thing/Place: Veo la casa, Visito Madrid, Conozco el hotel (zero 'a').
• Person: Veo a mi madre, Visito a mis padres, Conozco al profesor (personal 'a')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: veo la casa, veo a mi madre, visito Madrid, visito a mis padres, conozco al señor
exercises.meaning: I see the house (thing), I see my mother (person), I visit Madrid (city), I visit my parents (people), I know the gentleman (a + el)
exercises.explanation: Things and cities take zero 'a'; specific people take the personal 'a' (or al = a + el).

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I am going to visit my brother'?
options: Voy a visitar a mi hermano
exercises.target_answer: Voy a visitar a mi hermano
exercises.meaning: I am going to visit my brother
exercises.explanation: The first 'a' belongs to voy a + infinitive; the second 'a' is the personal 'a' before mi hermano!

exercises.idea: say that you want to invite your mother
cues: I want to invite → Quiero invitar
personal 'a' + my mother → a mi madre
idea_parts: I want to invite → Quiero invitar
my mother (with personal 'a') → a mi madre
exercises.meaning: I want to invite my mother

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.

summary.outcome: Place the personal 'a' (and contraction al) before specific human direct objects.

use_example.german: Visito Madrid y voy a visitar a mis padres.
use_example.english: I visit Madrid and I am going to visit my parents.

summary.takeaway: If the direct object is a specific person, put 'a' in front of them.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2302] Dative Pronoun Redundancy): see why Spanish loves doubling le/les with 'a + person'.

twist.explanation: a + el señor contracts to al señor: Veo al señor.

a.english_meaning: to, at (a + el = al; also personal 'a')
a.context_translation: I am going to the restaurant.
a.etymology_derivation: Fuses with masculine singular article el into al ('to the / at the').

ver.context_translation: I am going to see it/him today.
ver.etymology_derivation: Pronouns can hook directly onto the tail of the infinitive: verlo ('to see it/him')!

conocer.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places; conozco: I know)
conocer.shift_rule: 1st sg in -zco: conozco (takes personal 'a' before people!)
conocer.context_phrase: Conozco Madrid y conozco a tu hermano.
conocer.context_translation: I know Madrid and I know your brother.
conocer.etymology_derivation: Before a specific person, conhecer ALWAYS requires the personal 'a': conozco a María!

invitar.etymology_derivation: invitación → invitar. Pronouns hook onto the infinitive: quiero invitarlo ('I want to invite him/it').

visitar.etymology_derivation: visitation → visitar. No preposition 'to' needed in Spanish: quiero visitar (two words where English needs three).

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

padre.etymology_derivation: Plural los padres means 'the parents' (mother and father together).

hotel.etymology_derivation: Silent initial H. Latin hospitāle gives both 'hospital' and 'hotel'.
